name: Felix Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a blast-hole drill at an open-pit gold mine. The surveyors mark out a pattern of holes on the bench, and I walk the rig from mark to mark and drill each one about twelve metres down so the blast crew can load them. It's slow, loud and dusty, and I'm still getting the hang of reading the rock through the controls, when to ease off so I don't jam the bit. I like the routine. Same rig, same bench, same thermos of coffee every morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things for you money-wise and at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm fine, really. I live with Rosa, she cuts hair in town, and we rent a decent place. I've got about nine months of pay saved and a paid-off truck, and my grandfather left me a bit of land outside town that we might build on one day. There are a couple of other gold mines and a quarry near here, so drillers can usually find work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd bet on, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing I say now, which is not much. At the crib table I'd say I never saw the fuss. I don't really go online about anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep drilling and I get better at it. In a year or two I'd hope to stop jamming bits and get my speed up. That's my whole plan, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the drill job, keep saving the same amount, and maybe start thinking about building on the land in three or four years. I wouldn't change anything. I'm not someone who changes things for no reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Good, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any pressure at the mine already, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gold price is high right now, so the mine's happy. When it drops, they slow the drilling and cut overtime. I've only been here two years, so I haven't seen a bad year yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the land?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build a small house, nothing fancy. My grandfather left me a block of land outside town, and in the slow version I'd build a small house there with Rosa (my girlfriend).

say: I'd say at crib that I **never saw the fuss** about AI.
I'd keep **quiet online**, as I always do.
think: He'd keep drilling and **improve his speed** in a year or two.
A **gold price drop** is the only real pressure he sees.
do: Keep the **drill job** on the same bench.
Keep **saving** the same amount each pay.
Plan to **build on the land** in three or four years.
S0.quote: My grandfather left me a block of land outside town, and in the slow version I'd build a small house there with Rosa (my girlfriend).
fieldNote: His **savings and land**, plus a paid-off truck, make him genuinely secure.
He hasn't seen a **bad gold year** yet, which he admits.
He resists change **for its own sake**, a strong pattern.

steps.text: Keep drilling the same bench pattern on the gold mine rig
Keep saving the same amount from each pay
Build a small house on his grandfather's land in a few years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. They already have drills that run on their own at some mines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work it's not the end of the world, mines have always changed. With friends I'd say the office people are in trouble, not us. I'd keep it calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I know drills are one of the first machines they automate, because it's a pattern, the same thing over and over. I'm junior, so if they get two autonomous rigs, I'm the one who goes back to the water cart. Drilling is the same hole over and over, which is exactly the kind of work a robot rig takes first at a gold mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving and I'd hold off on building the house for now. I'd stay on the drill as long as they let me. If they moved me to a water cart or a truck, I'd take it rather than leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. I don't like it, and I don't know what to do about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says thinking tasks go first. What does that mean at your mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drill pattern design, the scheduling, the paperwork for the blast. If software does that, the engineer has fewer people under him. It doesn't change my rig right away, but it makes it easier to bolt automation onto it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the automation side yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. I'm slow with new technology, and I don't use any of the AI stuff. I'd learn it if they made me.

feel: **Worried**, without knowing what to do about it.

fieldNote: His public **calm** hides real fear of losing the drill.
He'd learn automation **only if forced**, true to his resistant style.
He sees software planning as making **automation easier** to bolt on.

steps.text: Hold off building the house on his grandfather's land

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's too fast. Two years? Come on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's crazy and someone needs to slow it down. At work I'd say we'll still need people for a while. To Rosa I'd say we'll be fine, because we have money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the drill's gone by 2031 at the latest. AI does the drill planning in 2028, then the robots take the rig. By 2031 the drill rig would run itself, and I'd have five years of a trade nobody needs anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back on spending, no big trips, no new truck. I'd look for another hands-on job, maybe at the quarry or in construction. I'd keep the land as a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd be up at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rosa?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're okay for a year or two. She'd say her salon's fine because robots can't cut hair, and maybe she's right. That would make her the steady one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to use AI tools now, to get ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I wouldn't know where to start. I'd rather find another job with my hands.

say: It's **too fast**, and someone needs to slow it down.
I'd tell Rosa we'll be **fine** because we have money.
think: The **drill rig** goes by 2031, after AI takes the planning in 2028.
He'd have **five years** in a trade nobody needs.
do: Cut **big spending**: no trips, no new truck.
Look for **hands-on work** at the quarry or in construction.
Keep the **land** as a safety net.
S2.quote: By 2031 the drill rig would run itself, and I'd have five years of a trade nobody needs anymore.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the drill job** and has no route into new tech.
Rosa's **salon** becomes the household's steadier income.
He'd **refuse** AI tools even with warning.

steps.text: Cancel trips and keep driving the paid-off truck
Apply for hands-on jobs at the quarry or in construction
Keep the land unsold as a safety net

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AI, eight for the robots. Still fast, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort things out, but someone needs to plan it. I'd say it at the crib table and to my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I'd have the drill job until about 2034, which is a long time for me. But I'd still need a plan for after. Eight years is long enough for me to get good at drilling and then watch a robot rig take my place anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder and maybe get a second ticket, like the excavator, which my boss keeps suggesting. I'd build the house on the land because it'd be paid off before the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less. I'd have time to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why build the house now, if things are changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a house you own is safe when work isn't. If I lose the job in 2034, at least we won't pay rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at any new kind of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe something like a mechanic. But I'd wait to see what's still around in a few years.

say: There's **time** to sort things out, but it needs a **plan**.
I'd say so at the **crib table** and to my dad.
think: He'd keep the drill until **about 2034**, which feels long.
He still expects a **robot rig** to replace him eventually.
do: Save harder and get an **excavator ticket**.
Build the **house on the land** so it's paid off before 2034.
feel: **Worried, but less**, with time to think.
S3.quote: Eight years is long enough for me to get good at drilling and then watch a robot rig take my place anyway.
fieldNote: He sees owning a **house** as safety against job loss.
He'd still **wait and see** on new careers.
His job loss is **expected but distant**, giving some control.

steps.text: Get an excavator ticket as his boss suggests
Build the house on his grandfather's land
Wait a few years before choosing a new trade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no point worrying yet. At work I'd tell the guys to keep their heads down. I'd keep quiet online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the drill's mine until 2039, which is basically a career. Thirteen years on the same drill rig would be fine by me, and after that I'd be 40 and could still learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep drilling, keep saving, and build the house in a few years. I'd only change if the mine pushed me. Maybe get one more ticket in the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A little on my mind, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw robots at the mine down the road. Seeing it would make it real for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger miner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a few tickets and save money. That's what I'd say.

say: There's **no point worrying** yet about something ten years off.
I'd tell the crew to **keep their heads down** and keep working.
think: The **drill job** lasts until 2039, which is basically a whole career.
At **40** he could still learn a new trade.
do: Build the **house** in a few years.
Get **one more ticket** in the next few years.
feel: **Mostly fine**, with it a little on his mind.
S4.quote: Thirteen years on the same drill rig would be fine by me, and after that I'd be 40 and could still learn a trade.
fieldNote: Ten years matches his **slow pace**, so he relaxes.
He'd change only after **seeing robots** nearby.
His advice to younger miners is **tickets and savings**, the same as his own plan.

steps.text: Keep drilling on the gold mine rig

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I wouldn't have time to learn anything new, and I'm slow at that. What would help is the company keeping juniors on other machines and a bit of paid training. I'm not good with new technology, so what would save me is time, not a course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the land. It's what makes me feel safe, more than the savings. Something to fall back on.

headlineQuote: I'm not good with new technology, so what would save me is time, not a course.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old** blast-hole drill operator at an open-pit gold mine, still learning.
He lives with Rosa, a hairdresser, and has **nine months saved** plus inherited land.
He's **pragmatic** and slow to change, and never uses AI tools.
He sees his repetitive drill job as **early for automation**, and fears that.
His mood moves from **calm** in the plateau to **alarmed** if AGI arrives by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no time to learn anything new.
whatWouldHelp: The company **keeping juniors** on other machines, plus a bit of **paid training**.
